deep.reconstruction:
This folio is not a Riemann manuscript. It is a German letter in Kurrent script, dated 'Leipzig 29/10 1894' and beginning 'Lieber Freund!'. It was evidently filed in the R.Varia bundle because it discusses a letter by Riemann. The previous page, a page of Macaulay's History of England, is unrelated. The next page continues this letter.

The writer has read a Riemann letter, which he returns with this one. He says that in it Riemann raises exactly the objections to Gauss's presentation of Pfaff's method that he himself had argued in detail, without naming Gauss, in Math. Annalen XVII pp. 523-530. Despite this, he advises against publishing Riemann's letter, for three reasons:
- it refers to an earlier oral or written communication and cannot be understood without a long commentary;
- he cannot tell what one passage near the opening refers to;
- Riemann returns to his objections only in sketchy form.

He conjectures that Riemann sent the letter as a 'feeler' to see whether Gauss would be offended by his rebuttals. Had Gauss encouraged him, Riemann would gladly have worked them out fully and published them. The Leipzig location and the Annalen reference strongly suggest the writer is Adolph Mayer, but this is my inference. The recipient may be one of the editors of Riemann's Werke (Weber, or the Nachträge editors) or Klein; unsure.

The only mathematical content on the page is the start of the writer's summary of the issue. Pfaff's solution of the Pfaff problem rests on repeating one and the same coordinate transformation. Gauss sets this out in Werke III pp. 237-241, in his 1815 review of Pfaff's 'Methodus generalis'.

In modern terms (my gloss, using the next page): given a Pfaffian form Omega = sum_{k=0}^{n-1} p_k dx_k, introduce new variables x, y_0, ..., y_{n-2} such that Omega = lambda * sum_{i=0}^{n-2} q_i(y) dy_i. That is, the form is reduced, up to a factor, to a form in one fewer variable. Iterating this gives Pfaff's reduction to a normal form. The objection, developed on the next page, is that Pfaff's method needs this step to be possible for even n, and Gauss does not prove it. No derivation is carried out on this page.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page: it is a descriptive letter.
The bibliographic references (Math. Ann. XVII pp. 523-530; Gauss Werke III pp. 237-241 and p. 232) are plausible but not verified here.

results.what: Description of Pfaff's method for the Pfaff problem: repeated transformation of a Pfaffian form in n variables to lambda times a form in n-1 variables.
results.modern_name: Pfaff problem / reduction of a Pfaffian form to normal form (Pfaff-Darboux theorem)
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Pfaff (1815); later Jacobi, Clebsch, Frobenius (1877), Darboux (1882)

results.what: Historical claim that Riemann wrote a letter (apparently to Gauss) objecting to Gauss's presentation of Pfaff's method, anticipating the 1894 writer's (probably A. Mayer's) Annalen critique.
results.modern_name: Correspondence on the foundations of Pfaff's method
results.usually_credited_to: Critique usually attributed to A. Mayer (Math. Ann. XVII)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is an 1894 letter by a later mathematician (probably Adolph Mayer), not Riemann's own mathematics. Its only interest is the archival note that Riemann had written a letter critical of Gauss's treatment of Pfaff's method. That is a minor historical detail and the letter itself is not shown here.

checkable.asserts: Illustration of the n=2 case (my example, not on the page): with integrating factor exp(x0), the form x1*dx0 + dx1 equals exp(-x0)*d(x1*exp(x0)); this is the dx0 component (should be 0).

transcription_corrections: The page is a letter dated Leipzig 29/10 1894, not a Riemann manuscript; the 'previous page' (Macaulay) is unrelated filing context.
The machine transcription of the body text appears essentially correct ('abgeschickt' is a plausible reading of 'abge-schickt').

The rotated left-margin footnote '*)' is only partially legible. It appears to qualify the Gauss Werke III reference (Gauss's remarks on the matter in his review); the transcription '... Anzeige' is uncertain.
